hook: A ramp that meets the floor at a sharp angle jolts a skateboard; a ramp that curves smoothly into the floor does not. Both are connected, with no gap to jump. Calculus draws the same line: a graph can be connected, continuous, and still have a point where no single slope exists.

chain.cause: The left and right difference quotients approach different numbers (a corner)
chain.effect: the two-sided limit does not exist and $f'(a)$ does not exist, even though $f$ may be continuous

chain.cause: The difference quotients grow without bound (a cusp or a vertical tangent)
chain.effect: there is no finite slope, so $f'(a)$ does not exist

ideas: $f$ is differentiable at $a$ when $f'(a)$ exists: the limit of the difference quotient is a finite number.
Differentiable implies continuous. In a justification, say it: "$f$ is differentiable at $a$, so $f$ is continuous at $a$."

Continuous does NOT imply differentiable. A continuous graph fails to have a derivative at a corner (one-sided slopes differ), a cusp (slopes become infinite in opposite directions) or a vertical tangent line.
Not continuous implies not differentiable: a jump, hole or asymptote rules out a derivative.
For a piecewise function at the break: check continuity first, then compare the left and right slopes.

misconception.wrong: The graph of $|x - 3|$ has no break at $x = 3$, so it has a derivative there.
misconception.right: No break means continuous, which is necessary but not enough. At $x = 3$ the slope is $-1$ from the left and 1 from the right, so the difference quotient has no limit: $|x - 3|$ is continuous but not differentiable at 3.

summary: A function is differentiable at $a$ when $f'(a)$ exists. Differentiability implies continuity, but not the other way round: corners, cusps and vertical tangents are continuous points with no derivative, and any discontinuity also rules a derivative out. At a break in a piecewise function, check continuity, then compare the one-sided slopes.
